# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0.23/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# proc_macro2_diagnostics - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2-diagnostics/^0.10/

## Expand description

Diagnostic emulation on stable and nightly.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

- Depend on the library in your proc-macro.

```
[dependencies]
proc_macro2_diagnostics = "0.10"
```
- Import `SpanDiagnosticExt``proc_macro2::Span``Diagnostic`

```
use syn::spanned::Spanned;
use proc_macro2::TokenStream;
use proc_macro2_diagnostics::{SpanDiagnosticExt, Diagnostic};
fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> Result<TokenStream, Diagnostic> {
    Err(input.span().error("there's a problem here..."))
}
```
- If there’s an error, emit the diagnostic as tokens:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro]
pub fn real_macro(tokens: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    match my_macro(tokens.into()) {
        Ok(tokens) => tokens.into(),
        Err(diag) => diag.emit_as_expr_tokens().into()
    }
}
```
This does the right thing on nightly *or* stable.

[§](https://docs.rs#caveats)Caveats

On stable, due to limitations, any top-level, non-error diagnostics are
emitted as errors. This will abort compilation. To avoid this, you may want
to `cfg`-gate emitting non-error diagnostics to nightly.

[§](https://docs.rs#colors)Colors

By default, error messages are colored on stable. To disable, disable default features:

```
[dependencies]
proc_macro2_diagnostics = { version = "0.10", default-features = false }
```
The compiler always colors diagnostics on nightly.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/struct.Diagnostic.html)
- A structure representing a diagnostic message and associated children messages.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Level](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)
- An enum representing a diagnostic level.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Span](https://docs.rs/trait.SpanDiagnosticExt.html)- Diagnostic - Ext
- Extension trait for `proc_macro2::Span`emulating the proc-macro diagnostic API on stable and nightly.

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0.7/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Abi](https://docs.rs/struct.Abi.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The binary interface of a function: `extern "C"`.
- [Angle](https://docs.rs/struct.AngleBracketedGenericArguments.html)- Bracketed - Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed arguments of a path segment: the `<K, V>`in`HashMap<K, V>`.
- [Arm](https://docs.rs/struct.Arm.html)- `full`
- One arm of a `match`expression:`0..=10 => { return true; }`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocConst.html)- Const - `derive`or- `full`
- An equality constraint on an associated constant: the `PANIC = false`in`Trait<PANIC = false>`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A binding (equality constraint) on an associated type: the `Item = u8`in`Iterator<Item = u8>`.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.Attribute.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An attribute, like `#[repr(transparent)]`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareFnArg.html)- FnArg - `derive`or- `full`
- An argument in a function type: the `usize`in`fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareVariadic.html)- Variadic - `derive`or- `full`
- The variadic argument of a function pointer like `fn(usize, ...)`.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)- `full`
- A braced block containing Rust statements.
- [Bound](https://docs.rs/struct.BoundLifetimes.html)- Lifetimes - `derive`or- `full`
- A set of bound lifetimes: `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A const generic parameter: `const LENGTH: usize`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.Constraint.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An associated type bound: `Iterator<Item: Display>`.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataEnum.html)- Enum - `derive`
- An enum input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`
- A struct input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataUnion.html)- Union - `derive`
- An untagged union input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Derive](https://docs.rs/struct.DeriveInput.html)- Input - `derive`
- Data structure sent to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error returned when a Syn parser cannot parse the input tokens.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprArray.html)- Array - `full`

- A binary operation: `a + b`,`a += b`.

- A blocked scope: `{ ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBreak.html)- Break - `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCall.html)- Call - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprContinue.html)- Continue - `full`
- A `continue`, with an optional label.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprField.html)- Field - `derive`or- `full`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attr](https://docs.rs/enum.AttrStyle.html)- Style - `derive`or- `full`
- Distinguishes between attributes that decorate an item and attributes that are contained within an item.
- [BinOp](https://docs.rs/enum.BinOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operator: `+`,`+=`,`&`.
- [Captured](https://docs.rs/enum.CapturedParam.html)- Param - `full`
- Single parameter in a precise capturing bound.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/enum.Data.html)- `derive`
- The storage of a struct, enum or union data structure.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A Rust expression.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldMutability.html)- Mutability - `derive`or- `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Fields](https://docs.rs/enum.Fields.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Data stored within an enum variant or struct.
- [FnArg](https://docs.rs/enum.FnArg.html)- `full`
- An argument in a function signature: the `n: usize`in`fn f(n: usize)`.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/enum.ForeignItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an `extern`block.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericArgument.html)- Argument - `derive`or- `full`
- An individual generic argument, like `'a`,`T`, or`Item = T`.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A generic type parameter, lifetime, or const generic: `T: Into<String>`,`'a: 'b`,`const LEN: usize`.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplRestriction.html)- Restriction - `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/enum.Item.html)- `full`
- Things that can appear directly inside of a module or scope.
- [Lit](https://docs.rs/enum.Lit.html)
- A Rust literal such as a string or integer or boolean.
- [Macro](https://docs.rs/enum.MacroDelimiter.html)- Delimiter - `derive`or- `full`
- A grouping token that surrounds a macro body: `m!(...)`or`m!{...}`or`m![...]`.
- [Member](https://docs.rs/enum.Member.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A struct or tuple struct field accessed in a struct literal or field expression.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/enum.Meta.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Content of a compile-time structured attribute.
- [Pat](https://docs.rs/enum.Pat.html)- `full`
- A pattern in a local binding, function signature, match expression, or various other places.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/enum.PathArguments.html)- Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed or parenthesized arguments of a path segment.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/enum.PointerMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- Mutability of a raw pointer (`*const T`,`*mut T`), in which non-mutable isn’t the implicit default.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/enum.RangeLimits.html)- Limits - `full`
- Limit types of a range, inclusive or exclusive.
- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- Return type of a function signature.
- [Static](https://docs.rs/enum.StaticMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- The mutability of an `Item::Static`or`ForeignItem::Static`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)- `full`
- A statement, usually ending in a semicolon.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitBoundModifier.html)- Bound - Modifier - `derive`or- `full`
- A modifier on a trait bound, currently only used for the `?`in`?Sized`.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item declaration within the definition of a trait.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The possible types that a Rust value could have.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeParamBound.html)- Param - Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait or lifetime used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [UnOp](https://docs.rs/enum.UnOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A unary operator: `*`,`!`,`-`.
- [UseTree](https://docs.rs/enum.UseTree.html)- `full`
- A suffix of an import tree in a `use`item:`Type as Renamed`or`*`.
- [Visibility](https://docs.rs/enum.Visibility.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The visibility level of an item: inherited or `pub`or`pub(restricted)`.
- [Where](https://docs.rs/enum.WherePredicate.html)- Predicate - `derive`or- `full`
- A single predicate in a `where`clause:`T: Deserialize<'de>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)- `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse tokens of source code into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse2](https://docs.rs/fn.parse2.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a proc-macro2 token stream into the chosen syntax tree node.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_file.html)- file - `full`and- `parsing`
- Parse the content of a file of Rust code.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_str.html)- str - `parsing`
- Parse a string of Rust code into the chosen syntax tree node.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- The result of a Syn parser.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# facett_video - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-video/0.1.10/facett_video/

## Expand description

**facett-video** (§22) — a video player whose chrome (transport, play/pause,
scrubber, volume, time, fullscreen) is **themed** and driven by the shared
[ KeyMap](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/look/keymap/struct.KeyMap.html); decode is a

**pluggable backend**trait (

[). M2 ships the](https://docs.rs/trait.FrameSource.html)

`FrameSource`[frame-source backend (a consumer pushes RGBA frames → texture each frame →](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameSequence.html)

`FrameSequence``ui.image`) for image
sequences / sim / camera (VID-2). The optional `egui-video` FFmpeg backend is
a host-side feature (VID-1).Overlay-ready (annotations/HUD via §5); **ROI selection** like the grid’s
range select (VID-3). **Copy a frame** yields a typed
[ ClipPayload::Image](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/clip/enum.ClipPayload.html) (the M2 image-copy
Exit criterion).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameSequence.html)- Sequence
- The frame-source backend (VID-2): an in-memory RGBA image sequence a consumer pushes into. Deterministic → the player snapshots + tests headlessly.
- [Video](https://docs.rs/struct.VideoPlayer.html)- Player
- The video player. Owns transport state + position + ROI; the decode is a boxed
`FrameSource`**injected clock**(`advance(dt)`), so it is deterministic for snapshots.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Frame](https://docs.rs/trait.FrameSource.html)- Source
- A pluggable decode backend (VID-1): hands the player the current frame as an
egui `egui::ColorImage`

# facett_timeline - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-timeline/0.1.10/facett_timeline/

## Expand description

**facett-timeline** — a **swimlane Gantt**: a wall-clock time axis with stacked,
named lanes of bars, each bar optionally split into phase **segments**. The
single Spark-defining visual facett lacked — it covers the **Jobs event
timeline** (executor lifecycle + job/stage bars), the **per-stage task event
timeline** (segmented phase bars), and the **Lakeflow run Gantt**, all from one
engine-agnostic [ TimelineModel](https://docs.rs/model/struct.TimelineModel.html) (a host maps Spark’s
event log / REST API onto it; this crate never learns what a “stage” is).

Two halves, exactly like the rest of facett:

- `model`- `[t0,t1]`window) with its own offset/- `state_json`tests.
- `TimelineView`- `Facet`- `state_json`so a headless driver asserts the pixels as DATA.

[§](https://docs.rs#fc-contract)FC contract

- **Serializable state**(- `state_json`,- `portable_state`/- `load_state`): the active window + per-bar- `start_frac`/- `width_frac`+ the selection.
- `Msg`- `TimelineView::update`
- **Render-proof**: the painter, the headless- `layout`- `state_json`all read bar offsets from- **one**formula (- `TimelineModel::bar_fraction_in`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use model::`- [Bar](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Bar.html);
- `pub use model::`- [BarStatus](https://docs.rs/model/enum.BarStatus.html);
- `pub use model::`- [Lane](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Lane.html);
- `pub use model::`- [Segment](https://docs.rs/model/struct.Segment.html);
- `pub use model::`- [TASK_PHASES](https://docs.rs/model/constant.TASK_PHASES.html);
- `pub use model::`- [TimelineModel](https://docs.rs/model/struct.TimelineModel.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- The **engine-agnostic, normalized timeline model**— the neutral shape a host (knut / nornir viz) maps a Spark**jobs event timeline**, a**per-stage task timeline**, or a**Lakeflow run Gantt**onto, and the`TimelineView`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BarLayout](https://docs.rs/struct.BarLayout.html)
- A laid-out bar — the exact rect the painter fills for one `Bar``layout``state_json`reports their fractions — one source of truth.
- [Timeline](https://docs.rs/struct.TimelineView.html)- View
- The **swimlane Gantt**`Facet``TimelineModel`**id**(FC-5), and an optional zoom**window**over the model’s full span.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Msg](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)
- A robot-/CLI-addressable control message — the named boundary a headless driver
(or a host toolbar) drives the view through, the same effect the canvas gestures
produce. Applied by `TimelineView::update`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [layout](https://docs.rs/fn.layout.html)
- **Pure layout**— given the plotting- `content`rect (the area right of the lane gutter, below the time axis) and the active window- `[t0,t1]`, return one- `BarLayout`- `Ui`: a test calls this directly and asserts the bar rects (offsets + widths). The painter calls the SAME fn, so the asserted rects ARE the pixels.

# facett_table - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/facett_table/

## Expand description

**facett-table** — a generic **data-table** viewer: named columns + string
rows in a striped grid, with cell truncation + a row scroll. Generalised from
nornir’s warehouse table (“oslo”) — but source-agnostic (any `Vec<String>`
rows). A [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html); the consumer formats its cells to strings.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use warehouse::`- [PreviewTable](https://docs.rs/warehouse/struct.PreviewTable.html);
- `pub use warehouse::`- [WarehouseTableView](https://docs.rs/warehouse/struct.WarehouseTableView.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [warehouse](https://docs.rs/warehouse/index.html)
- The **warehouse browser**Facet — a multi-table picker + grid / auto bar-chart, generalised from nornir’s`src/viz/warehouse_tab.rs`(`WarehouseBrowser`) with the Iceberg/gRPC source abstracted away. See`warehouse::WarehouseTableView`**WarehouseTableView**— a generic warehouse-style data browser: a left**table picker**, and for the selected table either a striped grid OR (when a numeric column exists) a hand-painted horizontal**bar chart**, with combo pickers for the value/label columns. Generalised from nornir’s`src/viz/warehouse_tab.rs`(`WarehouseBrowser`).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Table](https://docs.rs/struct.Table.html)
- A data table: header `columns`+`rows`(each a row of cells).

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [RowId](https://docs.rs/type.RowId.html)
- A stable, domain-level identity for a row (FC-5). When present, selection is
keyed on this string instead of the visual `row.index()`, so an insert/delete that shifts visual positions does**not**silently move the selection.

# facett_tabbar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-tabbar/0.1.10/facett_tabbar/

## Expand description

**facett-tabbar** — the generic, themed **nav toolbar**: a control strip
(workspace/palette/About/live-style pickers + toggles, host-painted) plus a
two-row strip of tab headers, the active tab carrying the palette accent.
Adopted from nornir’s `src/viz/facett_ui.rs` (`TabBar` / `TabItem` /
`BarControl`) — the header of that file explicitly says it “should live in
the upstream `facett` crate”; the only thing that kept it in nornir is the
egui 0.33↔0.34 skew (egui-snarl pins 0.33). facett is on egui 0.34, so this
is the re-home; nornir re-points to `facett::tabbar::TabBar` once its viz
bumps to 0.34 (still gated on egui-snarl shipping 0.34 — see the cut policy
note in the batch report).

Two surfaces:

- `TabBar`- `&[TabItem]`+ an- `active`id), the verbatim port of nornir’s bar.- `show()`returns the id of the newly-clicked tab;- `state_json()`reports the tabs/active/split/controls.
- `TabBarView`- **owning**canonical- `Facet`- `local()`/- `remote()`,- `state_json()`,- `caps()`) so a- `FacetDeck`mounts the bar as a tab and a headless driver reads + drives the selection. It tracks its own- `active`and clicking a header re-keys it (and records the click count).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BarControl](https://docs.rs/struct.BarControl.html)
- A declarative descriptor of one **picker / toggle / button**the bar hosts in its left/right slots (workspace combo, palette combo, About toggle, live checkbox, …). The bar does NOT paint these — the host paints them through a slot closure — but the descriptor lets`state_json`report*which*controls are present and their values (the “components expose readable data” LAW) without the bar knowing anything domain-specific.
- [TabBar](https://docs.rs/struct.TabBar.html)
- The generic, themed **nav/toolbar**widget: a control strip plus a two-row strip of tab headers, all painted in the active`Theme``&[TabItem]`, the left/right slots are host-supplied closures, and the controls they host are declared as`BarControl`
- [TabBar](https://docs.rs/struct.TabBarView.html)- View
- An **owning**canonical`Facet``TabBar``tabs`+`active`+`controls`, paints the bar (no host slots — the controls are reported, not interactive here), tracks the live selection across frames, and exposes the whole rendered bar through`Facet::state_json`
- [TabItem](https://docs.rs/struct.TabItem.html)
- One tab in a `TabBar``id`(emitted in`state_json`+ matched on click) plus the human`label`egui paints on the header (icon + words, e.g.`"🔗 Dep Graph"`), so an AccessKit/robot click resolves by the same string the user reads. Keeping`id`and`label`separate lets a host rename a label without breaking click-by-id wiring or the`state_json`contract.
- [Underline](https://docs.rs/struct.UnderlineTween.html)- Tween
- Active-tab **underline slide**state (injected-clock, FC-7): holds the current eased underline rect, which each frame eases toward the active tab’s rect. Held by the owning`TabBarView``TabBar::show_anim`

# facett_syschart - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-syschart/0.1.10/facett_syschart/

## Expand description

**facett-syschart** — a **system-map chart**: a handful of *free-positioned*
peer nodes (not a layered DAG) joined by edges, each carrying a **badge**
(a count / status number) and, when selected, an **inline expandable detail
panel**. Click a node to select it; its detail renders in a panel under the
canvas. The host owns *what* a node’s detail is (a string here; richer hosts
draw their own widgets after `ui()` keyed off [ SystemChart::selected](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemChart.html#method.selected)).

This is the piece [ facett_core::draw](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/fn.draw.html)/[

`facett_graph::GraphView`] don’t
cover — those paint a *non-interactive*

`Scene`; `DepGraphView` is a
*layered*DAG with a fixed deps/dependents drill-down. A “monitoring map” of a few peer systems (a PKI/OIDC/Nexus triangle, a service mesh) wants deterministic positions, a per-node badge, click-select, and a free-form detail panel — that’s

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemChart.html)

`SystemChart`Like every facett component it implements [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html):

`title` / `ui` /
`state_json` (every node, badge, edge + the selection), so it drops into a
`FacetDeck` and is robot-testable through `facett_core::harness` — drive
[headlessly and assert](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemChart.html#method.select)

`SystemChart::select``state_json`.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [SysEdge](https://docs.rs/struct.SysEdge.html)
- An undirected link between two node ids.
- [SysNode](https://docs.rs/struct.SysNode.html)
- One system in the map. Positions are **normalized**(`0.0..=1.0`of the canvas), so the layout is resolution-independent and deterministic — ideal for headless rendering and screenshots.
- [System](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemChart.html)- Chart
- The system-map chart: nodes + edges + the current selection.

# facett_stat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-stat/0.1.10/facett_stat/

## Expand description

**facett-stat** — the generic, *non-domain* viz stat widgets factored out of
nornir’s `src/viz/facett_ui.rs` (status chips, a health pill, themed
sparklines) and the inline-bar stat table from `src/viz/mcp_tab.rs`. The
nornir originals lived in the viz crate only because of an egui-version skew
(the viz is pinned to egui 0.33 by `egui-snarl`, facett is on 0.34) — the
header of `facett_ui.rs` says verbatim *“These widgets … should live in the
upstream  facett crate”*. facett is already on 0.34, so this is the re-home.

Two layers:

- **Free painter helpers**—- `status_verdict`- `sparkline`- `health_pill`- `egui::Painter`
- `StatGridView`- `Facet`- `StatRow`- `local()`/- `remote()`/- `state_json()`/- `caps()`so the deck + test matrix discover it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Stat](https://docs.rs/struct.StatGridView.html)- Grid - View
- A stat table: each row a label + inline bar + optional sparkline + verdict
chip. A canonical `Facet`
- [StatRow](https://docs.rs/struct.StatRow.html)
- One row of a `StatGridView`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html)
- A generic status **verdict**— the small vocabulary panes map their domain status onto (pass/fail/skip/ignore/running). Mirrors nornir’s`status_chip`.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [AMBER](https://docs.rs/constant.AMBER.html)
- The amber used for running/stalled verdicts + the mid health band.
- [RED](https://docs.rs/constant.RED.html)
- The warm red used across facett for failure/negative (no semantic red in the base palette) — shared by the verdict chip + the health ramp.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [health_](https://docs.rs/fn.health_color.html)- color
- The red→amber→green health colour for a 0–100 score (the ramp nornir’s theme bakes in; inlined so facett-stat needs no extra theme surface).
- [health_](https://docs.rs/fn.health_pill.html)- pill
- A 0–100 **health pill**on a red→amber→green ramp. Port of nornir’s`viz::facett_ui::health_pill`(its`Theme::health_color`ramp inlined here so the widget is self-contained — facett-core’s`Theme`carries no health ramp).
- [sparkline](https://docs.rs/fn.sparkline.html)
- A tiny themed **sparkline**of a value series (line = palette`point`). Values self-normalize; higher = up. No-op for <2 points. Direct port of nornir’s`viz::facett_ui::sparkline`.
- [status_](https://docs.rs/fn.status_verdict.html)- verdict
- `(tag, colour)`for a free-text status on the active theme — the direct port of nornir’s- `viz::facett_ui::status_chip`. An unknown status is- `("?", dim)`.

# facett_plotters - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-plotters/0.1.10/facett_plotters/

## Expand description

**facett-plotters** — the chart types [ egui_plot](https://docs.rs/egui_plot)
(→

`facett-plot`) *lacks*, painted in

**immediate mode**directly on an

[.](https://docs.rs/egui/0.34.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/egui/painter/struct.Painter.html)

`egui::Painter``egui_plot` already covers line/scatter/bar/histogram with
zoom/pan; this crate fills the analytics long-tail Plotly defines:- `BoxPlotView`
- `ViolinView`
- `HeatmapView`
- `CandlestickView`
- `TreemapView`

[§](https://docs.rs#why-hand-rolled-not-the-plotters-crate)Why hand-rolled, not the `plotters` crate

The `plotters` crate is **retained + raster/SVG-backend driven**: its egui
integration renders to a bitmap and blits a texture every frame, with no
immediate-mode hit-testing, no live theming, and no hover model. facett’s
charts must read [`facett_core::theme`] live (re-skin on theme switch),
expose cheap hover-readouts, and implement the [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)
contract (

`caps()` + `copy()` → CSV). Hand-painting on the egui `Painter`
(the same path `facett-core`/`facett-map` use) is the lighter, better-fitting
choice — so `plotters` is *not*a dependency.

[§](https://docs.rs#theme-derived-colour-ramps)Theme-derived colour ramps

No palette is hardcoded. [ ramp::Ramp](https://docs.rs/ramp/struct.Ramp.html) builds a

**sequential**(

`bg`→`accent`→`glow`) or **diverging**(

`accent`→`text_dim`→`glow`) ramp
purely from the active [, so heatmaps/treemaps follow whatever theme is set.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/theme/struct.Theme.html)

`Theme`Each view is a [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html): it declares

`caps().themeable().copyable().resizable()`, paints itself, and `copy()`
emits the underlying data as CSV. The data→geometry math (quartiles, KDE
bins, OHLC mapping, heatmap cell layout, treemap squarify) lives in **pure, tested functions**that need no GPU.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use boxplot::`- [BoxPlotView](https://docs.rs/boxplot/struct.BoxPlotView.html);
- `pub use boxplot::`- [Quartiles](https://docs.rs/boxplot/struct.Quartiles.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [CandlestickView](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.CandlestickView.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [Ohlc](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.Ohlc.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [OhlcLayout](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.OhlcLayout.html);
- `pub use heatmap::`- [HeatmapView](https://docs.rs/heatmap/struct.HeatmapView.html);
- `pub use ramp::`- [Ramp](https://docs.rs/ramp/struct.Ramp.html);
- `pub use treemap::`- [Tile](https://docs.rs/treemap/struct.Tile.html);
- `pub use treemap::`- [TreemapView](https://docs.rs/treemap/struct.TreemapView.html);
- `pub use violin::`- [Density](https://docs.rs/violin/struct.Density.html);
- `pub use violin::`- [ViolinView](https://docs.rs/violin/struct.ViolinView.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [boxplot](https://docs.rs/boxplot/index.html)
- **Box plot**— quartiles + whiskers + outliers, one box per named group. The data→geometry math (- `Quartiles::from_sorted`- `Quartiles::compute`- `BoxPlotView`- `Facet`
- [candlestick](https://docs.rs/candlestick/index.html)
- **Candlestick**(OHLC) chart. Each bar is an open/high/low/close tuple drawn as a wick (high→low) + a body (open↔close), coloured up/down from theme colours. The price→pixel mapping (- `OhlcLayout`
- [heatmap](https://docs.rs/heatmap/index.html)
- **Heatmap**— a- `rows × cols`matrix painted as a colour grid using a theme-derived- `Ramp`- `cell_rect`
- [ramp](https://docs.rs/ramp/index.html)
- **Theme-derived colour ramps.**No hardcoded palette: a sequential ramp is built from the theme’s- `bg`→- `accent`→- `glow`, and a diverging ramp from- `accent`(low) through a neutral midpoint to- `glow`(high). Charts call- `Ramp::at`- `t ∈ 0..=1`to map a scalar to a colour.
- [treemap](https://docs.rs/treemap/index.html)
- **Treemap**— weighted rectangles, area ∝ value, laid out by a deterministic- **slice-and-dice**algorithm that alternates split direction by depth-of-cut so the tiling stays readable. The layout (- `squarify`- `(index, Rect)`pairs, tested independently of any painter. Tile fills come from a theme-derived sequential- `Ramp`
- [violin](https://docs.rs/violin/index.html)
- **Violin plot**— a mirrored kernel-density silhouette per group. The KDE (- `kde`- `ViolinView`

# gitwig 2.3.15 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/gitwig/2.3.15

# 🌿 Gitwig — Terminal Git UI & SourceTree Alternative (Built in Rust)

**Gitwig** (derived from **Git** + **Twig**, representing repository branches) is a lightweight, keyboard-driven **Terminal Git UI** (TUI) designed as a fast, minimal alternative to desktop Git GUI clients like **SourceTree** and terminal clients like **lazygit**. Built with Rust and `ratatui`, Gitwig presents all your Git repositories, worktrees, stashes, and branches in a clean, interactive bordered layout directly inside your terminal window.

## 🚀 Installation & Running

### Prerequisites

**Gitwig** requires the following external tools to be installed on your system:

- `git`- `git`is required in your- `PATH`for operations like staging, diffing, pushing, pulling, and network syncing.
- `ssh`- [!NOTE] - **SSH Host Key Policy:**To prevent connection hangs in the non-interactive TUI context, Gitwig executes git commands with- `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`set to- `ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`. This automatically trusts and saves new host keys, while verifying existing ones to protect against MITM attacks. If you require a different SSH policy, make sure to add host keys to your- `known_hosts`beforehand.

#### Via Homebrew (macOS / Linux)

You can tap and install **Gitwig** using Homebrew:

```
```
*Note: If Homebrew prompts you with an "untrusted tap" error, run  brew trust tareqmy/gitwig to trust it, and then run brew install gitwig again.*

#### Via Shell Script (macOS / Linux)

For a quick installation, run the following command in your terminal:

```
 |
```
#### On Windows

You can install **Gitwig** on Windows via PowerShell:

Run the following command in PowerShell:

```
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tareqmy/gitwig/master/scripts/install.ps1 | iex
```
- **Benefits**: Quick command-line installation to your user profile directory (- `%USERPROFILE%\.gitwig\bin`) without requiring administrator privileges.
- **Updating**: Supports the in-app self-updater, which will automatically run- `install.ps1`to download newer versions.

#### Via Chocolatey (Windows)

You can install **Gitwig** using Chocolatey:

```
choco install gitwig
```
*Note: For the in-app self-updater, if installed via Chocolatey, you should update the package by running  choco upgrade gitwig.*

## ✨ Features

- **Fullscreen Terminal UI**: Designed using- `ratatui`and- `crossterm`with modern visual styling.
- **Config-Driven Layout**: Driven by- `config.toml`for persistence and custom configurations.
- **In-App Card Management**: Add, edit, delete, and label items directly from the UI with automatic disk persistence.
- **Global Summary Header Bar**: High-level dashboard stats showing aggregate counts of repos, dirty repos, ahead counts, and stale repos.
- **Background Auto-Refresh**: Non-blocking background status checking every 10 seconds to keep your repo cards live and up-to-date.
- **Uncommitted Work Warning Badge**: Highlights repositories with a- `⚠ PARTIAL`badge when staged and unstaged changes coexist simultaneously.
- **Fuzzy Jump Picker**: Instantly jump to any repository by name using the- `/`overlay.
- **Favorite / Star Repositories**: Bookmark important repositories with- `*`separate from pinned items.
- **Compact View Toggle**: Press- `v`to toggle between standard 4-row cards and a dense 1-row view.
- **Label / Group Collapsing**: Organize repositories on the home page with collapsible label headers.
- **Full-Screen Detail View**: Press- `Enter`to open a multi-tab inspection interface (Workspace, Files tree with preview, Graph log, Branches, Tags, Remotes, Stashes, Worktrees, Submodules, Reflog). Tab headers dynamically fallback to their first character under restricted widths to prevent overflow.
- **Mode-Aware Status Bar**: Shows contextual shortcuts dynamically with support for collapsed/expanded view (- `.`). When expanded, it dynamically wraps the shortcut items and calculates the exact number of rows needed based on terminal width.
