# rayon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rayon/^1.0/

## Expand description

Rayon is a data-parallelism library that makes it easy to convert sequential computations into parallel.

It is lightweight and convenient for introducing parallelism into existing code. It guarantees data-race free executions and takes advantage of parallelism when sensible, based on work-load at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-rayon)How to use Rayon

There are two ways to use Rayon:

- **High-level parallel constructs**are the simplest way to use Rayon and also typically the most efficient.- [Parallel iterators](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)make it easy to convert a sequential iterator to execute in parallel.- The `ParallelIterator`
- The `IndexedParallelIterator`

- The
- The `par_sort``&mut [T]`slices (or vectors) in parallel.
- `par_extend`

- **Custom tasks**let you divide your work into parallel tasks yourself.- `join`
- `scope`
- `ThreadPoolBuilder`

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-and-the-rayon-prelude)Basic usage and the Rayon prelude

First, you will need to add `rayon` to your `Cargo.toml`.

Next, to use parallel iterators or the other high-level methods,
you need to import several traits. Those traits are bundled into
the module [ rayon::prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html). It is recommended that you import
all of these traits at once by adding

`use rayon::prelude::*` at
the top of each module that uses Rayon methods.These traits give you access to the `par_iter` method which provides
parallel implementations of many iterative functions such as [ map](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.map),

[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.for_each)

`for_each`[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.filter)

`filter`[, and](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.fold)

`fold`[more](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#provided-methods).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-layout)Crate Layout

Rayon extends many of the types found in the standard library with
parallel iterator implementations. The modules in the `rayon`
crate mirror [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html) itself: so, e.g., the

`option` module in
Rayon contains parallel iterators for the `Option` type, which is
found in [the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/index.html). Similarly, the

`option` module of `std``collections` module in Rayon offers parallel iterator types for
[the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/index.html). You will rarely need to access these submodules unless you need to name iterator types explicitly.

`collections` from `std`[§](https://docs.rs#targets-without-threading)Targets without threading

Rayon has limited support for targets without `std` threading implementations.
See the [ rayon_core](https://docs.rs/rayon-core/1.13.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rayon_core/index.html) documentation for more information about its global fallback.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-questions)Other questions?

See [the Rayon FAQ](https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/main/FAQ.md).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html)
- Parallel iterator types for [arrays](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.array.html)(`[T; N]`)
- [collections](https://docs.rs/collections/index.html)
- Parallel iterator types for [standard collections](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/index.html)
- [iter](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)
- Traits for writing parallel programs using an iterator-style interface
- [option](https://docs.rs/option/index.html)
- Parallel iterator types for [options](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/index.html)
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- The rayon prelude imports the various `ParallelIterator`traits. The intention is that one can include`use rayon::prelude::*`and have easy access to the various traits and methods you will need.
- [range](https://docs.rs/range/index.html)
- Parallel iterator types for [ranges](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/range/struct.Range.html), the type for values created by`a..b`expressions
- [range_](https://docs.rs/range_inclusive/index.html)- inclusive
- Parallel iterator types for [inclusive ranges](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/range/struct.RangeInclusive.html), the type for values created by`a..=b`expressions
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Parallel iterator types for [results](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/index.html)
- [slice](https://docs.rs/slice/index.html)
- Parallel iterator types for [slices](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/slice/index.html)
- [str](https://docs.rs/str/index.html)
- Parallel iterator types for [strings](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/str/index.html)
- [string](https://docs.rs/string/index.html)
- This module contains the parallel iterator types for owned strings
(`String`). You will rarely need to interact with it directly unless you have need to name one of the iterator types.
- [vec](https://docs.rs/vec/index.html)
- Parallel iterator types for [vectors](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/index.html)(`Vec<T>`)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Broadcast](https://docs.rs/struct.BroadcastContext.html)- Context
- Provides context to a closure called by `broadcast`.
- [FnContext](https://docs.rs/struct.FnContext.html)
- Provides the calling context to a closure called by `join_context`.
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/struct.Scope.html)
- Represents a fork-join scope which can be used to spawn any number of tasks.
See `scope()`
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeFifo.html)- Fifo
- Represents a fork-join scope which can be used to spawn any number of tasks.
Those spawned from the same thread are prioritized in relative FIFO order.
See `scope_fifo()`
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadBuilder.html)- Builder
- Thread builder used for customization via `ThreadPoolBuilder::spawn_handler()`
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadPool.html)- Pool
- Represents a user-created [thread pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thread_pool).
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadPoolBuildError.html)- Pool - Build - Error
- Error when initializing a thread pool.
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadPoolBuilder.html)- Pool - Builder
- Used to create a new `ThreadPool`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Yield](https://docs.rs/enum.Yield.html)
- Result of `yield_now()``yield_local()`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [broadcast](https://docs.rs/fn.broadcast.html)
- Executes `op`within every thread in the current thread pool. If this is called from a non-Rayon thread, it will execute in the global thread pool. Any attempts to use`join`,`scope`, or parallel iterators will then operate within that thread pool. When the call has completed on each thread, returns a vector containing all of their return values.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the number of threads in the current registry. If this code is executing within a Rayon thread pool, then this will be the number of threads for the thread pool of the current thread. Otherwise, it will be the number of threads for the global thread pool.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_thread_index.html)- thread_ - index
- If called from a Rayon worker thread, returns the index of that
thread within its current pool; if not called from a Rayon thread,
returns `None`.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope.html)- place_ - scope
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope_fifo.html)- place_ - scope_ - fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [join](https://docs.rs/fn.join.html)
- Takes two closures and *potentially*runs them in parallel. It returns a pair of the results from those closures.
- [join_](https://docs.rs/fn.join_context.html)- context
- Identical to `join`, except that the closures have a parameter that provides context for the way the closure has been called, especially indicating whether they’re executing on a different thread than where`join_context`was called. This will occur if the second job is stolen by a different thread, or if`join_context`was called from outside the thread pool to begin with.
- [max_](https://docs.rs/fn.max_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the maximum number of threads that Rayon supports in a single thread pool.
- [scope](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [scope_](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)- fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [spawn](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn.html)
- Puts the task into the Rayon thread pool’s job queue in the “static”
or “global” scope. Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)to create a scope.`scope()`function
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_broadcast.html)- broadcast
- Spawns an asynchronous task on every thread in this thread pool. This task
will run in the implicit, global scope, which means that it may outlast the
current stack frame – therefore, it cannot capture any references onto the
stack (you will likely need a `move`closure).
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_fifo.html)- fifo
- Fires off a task into the Rayon thread pool in the “static” or
“global” scope.  Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)to create a scope.`scope_fifo()`function
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_local.html)- local
- Cooperatively yields execution to local Rayon work.
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_now.html)- now
- Cooperatively yields execution to Rayon.

# rustversion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustversion/^1/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]`[§](https://docs.rs#selectors)Selectors

- `#[rustversion::stable]`
 True on any stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`
 True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::beta]`
 True on any beta compiler.
- `#[rustversion::nightly]`
 True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
- `#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`
 True on exactly one nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`
 True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`
 True on that nightly and all newer ones.
- `#[rustversion::before(`- *version or date*- `)]`
 Negative of- *#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
- `#[rustversion::not(`- *selector*- `)]`
 Negative of any selector; for example- *#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
- `#[rustversion::any(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example- *#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
- `#[rustversion::all(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example- *#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
- `#[rustversion::attr(`- *selector*- `,`- *attribute*- `)]`
 For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to- `cfg_attr`.
- `rustversion::cfg!(`- *selector*- `)`
 An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example- *if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-cases)Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
use std::pin::Pin;
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
impl<P: MyTrait> MyTrait for Pin<P> {
    /* ... */
}
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
#[rustversion::attr(before(1.33), repr(packed))]
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.33), repr(packed(2)))]
struct Six(i16, i32);
fn main() {
    println!("{}", std::mem::align_of::<Six>());
}
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case
by the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.32), const)]
fn duration_as_days(dur: Duration) -> u64 {
    dur.as_secs() / 60 / 60 / 24
}
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
fn main() {
    if rustversion::cfg!(since(1.36)) {
        println!("cargo:rustc-cfg=no_std");
    }
}
```
```
// src/lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(no_std, no_std)]
#[cfg(no_std)]
extern crate alloc;
```

---

# tar - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tar/^0.4/

## Expand description

A library for reading and writing TAR archives

This library provides utilities necessary to manage [TAR archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tar_%28computing%29)
abstracted over a reader or writer. Great strides are taken to ensure that
an archive is never required to be fully resident in memory, and all objects
provide largely a streaming interface to read bytes from.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

When unpacking archives ([ Archive::unpack](https://docs.rs/struct.Archive.html#method.unpack),

[), a best-effort is made to prevent writing files outside the destination directory: paths containing](https://docs.rs/struct.Entry.html#method.unpack_in)

`Entry::unpack_in``..` are rejected, and symlink targets within
the archive are validated before use.**Concurrent mutation of the destination tree is outside the threat model.**
If another process modifies the destination (for example, by atomically
swapping a symlink) while extraction is in progress, this crate may follow
a path outside the intended destination. Preventing such TOCTOU races
requires OS primitives (e.g. `openat`/`O_PATH` used throughout) that this
crate does not use. When extracting untrusted archives in an environment
where the destination may be concurrently modified, use the [ cap-std](https://docs.rs/cap-std/)
crate and/or OS-level sandboxing.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Archive](https://docs.rs/struct.Archive.html)
- A top-level representation of an archive file.
- [Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html)
- A structure for building archives
- [Entries](https://docs.rs/struct.Entries.html)
- An iterator over the entries of an archive.
- [Entry](https://docs.rs/struct.Entry.html)
- A read-only view into an entry of an archive.
- [Entry](https://docs.rs/struct.EntryWriter.html)- Writer
- A writer for a single entry in a tar archive.
- [GnuExt](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuExtSparseHeader.html)- Sparse - Header
- Representation of the entry found to represent extended GNU sparse files.
- [GnuHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuHeader.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [GnuSparse](https://docs.rs/struct.GnuSparseHeader.html)- Header
- Description of the header of a sparse entry.
- [Header](https://docs.rs/struct.Header.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [OldHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.OldHeader.html)
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive
- [PaxExtension](https://docs.rs/struct.PaxExtension.html)
- A key/value pair corresponding to a pax extension.
- [PaxExtensions](https://docs.rs/struct.PaxExtensions.html)
- An iterator over the pax extensions in an archive entry.
- [Ustar](https://docs.rs/struct.UstarHeader.html)- Header
- Representation of the header of an entry in an archive

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Entry](https://docs.rs/enum.EntryType.html)- Type
- Indicate the type of content described by a header.
- [Header](https://docs.rs/enum.HeaderMode.html)- Mode
- Declares the information that should be included when filling a Header from filesystem metadata.
- [Unpacked](https://docs.rs/enum.Unpacked.html)
- When unpacking items the unpacked thing is returned to allow custom additional handling by users. Today the File is returned, in future the enum may be extended with kinds for links, directories etc.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DETERMINISTIC_](https://docs.rs/constant.DETERMINISTIC_TIMESTAMP.html)- TIMESTAMP
- A deterministic, arbitrary, non-zero timestamp that use used as `mtime`of headers when`HeaderMode::Deterministic`

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/proc-macro2/1.0.106/target-redirect/proc_macro2/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

                    There is very little structured metadata to build this page

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0.23/index.html

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. -
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# parse_macro_input in syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html

```
macro_rules! parse_macro_input {
    ($tokenstream:ident as $ty:ty) => { ... };
    ($tokenstream:ident with $parser:path) => { ... };
    ($tokenstream:ident) => { ... };
}
```
**crate features**only.

`parsing` and `proc-macro`## Expand description

Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.

Refer to the [ parse module](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html) documentation for more details about parsing
in Syn.

[§](https://docs.rs#intended-usage)Intended usage

This macro must be called from a function that returns
`proc_macro::TokenStream`. Usually this will be your proc macro entry point,
the function that has the #[proc_macro] / #[proc_macro_derive] /
#[proc_macro_attribute] attribute.

```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, Result};
use syn::parse::{Parse, ParseStream};
struct MyMacroInput {
    /* ... */
}
impl Parse for MyMacroInput {
    fn parse(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        /* ... */
    }
}
#[proc_macro]
pub fn my_macro(tokens: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(tokens as MyMacroInput);
    /* ... */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage-with-parser)Usage with Parser

This macro can also be used with the [ Parser trait](https://docs.rs/parse/trait.Parser.html) for types that have
multiple ways that they can be parsed.

```
impl MyMacroInput {
    fn parse_alternate(input: ParseStream) -> Result<Self> {
        /* ... */
    }
}
#[proc_macro]
pub fn my_macro(tokens: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    let input = parse_macro_input!(tokens with MyMacroInput::parse_alternate);
    /* ... */
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#expansion)Expansion

`parse_macro_input!($variable as $Type)` expands to something like:

```
match syn::parse::<$Type>($variable) {
    Ok(syntax_tree) => syntax_tree,
    Err(err) => return proc_macro::TokenStream::from(err.to_compile_error()),
}
```

`pub struct Group { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A delimited token stream.

A `Group` internally contains a `TokenStream` which is surrounded by
`Delimiter`s.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

This constructor will set the span for this group to

method below.

# Punct in proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0.23/struct.Punct.html

`pub struct Punct { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A `Punct` is a single punctuation character like `+`, `-` or `#`.

Multicharacter operators like `+=` are represented as two instances of
`Punct` with different forms of `Spacing` returned.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a new `Punct` from the given character and spacing.

The `ch` argument must be a valid punctuation character permitted by the
language, otherwise the function will panic.

The returned `Punct` will have the default span of `Span::call_site()`
which can be further configured with the `set_span` method below.

Returns the spacing of this punctuation character, indicating whether
it’s immediately followed by another `Punct` in the token stream, so
they can potentially be combined into a multicharacter operator
(`Joint`), or it’s followed by some other token or whitespace (`Alone`)
so the operator has certainly ended.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# Span in proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0.23/struct.Span.html

`pub struct Span { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

The span of the invocation of the current procedural macro.

Identifiers created with this span will be resolved as if they were written directly at the macro call location (call-site hygiene) and other code at the macro call site will be able to refer to them as well.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#422-424)#### pub fn [mixed_site](https://docs.rs#method.mixed_site)() -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#422-424)

#### pub fn [mixed_site](https://docs.rs#method.mixed_site)() -> Self

The span located at the invocation of the procedural macro, but with
local variables, labels, and `$crate` resolved at the definition site
of the macro. This is the same hygiene behavior as `macro_rules`.

A span that resolves at the macro definition site.

This method is semver exempt and not exposed by default.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#437-439)#### pub fn [resolved_at](https://docs.rs#method.resolved_at)(&self, other: [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)) -> [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#437-439)

Creates a new span with the same line/column information as `self` but
that resolves symbols as though it were at `other`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#443-445)

#### pub fn [located_at](https://docs.rs#method.located_at)(&self, other: [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)) -> [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

Creates a new span with the same name resolution behavior as `self` but
with the line/column information of `other`.

Convert `proc_macro2::Span` to `proc_macro::Span`.

This method is available when building with a nightly compiler, or when
building with rustc 1.29+ *without* semver exempt features.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if called from outside of a procedural macro. Unlike
`proc_macro2::Span`, the `proc_macro::Span` type can only exist within
the context of a procedural macro invocation.

**crate feature**only.

`span-locations`Returns the span’s byte position range in the source file.

This method requires the `"span-locations"` feature to be enabled.

When executing in a procedural macro context, the returned range is only accurate if compiled with a nightly toolchain. The stable toolchain does not have this information available. When executing outside of a procedural macro, such as main.rs or build.rs, the byte range is always accurate regardless of toolchain.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#564-566)#### pub fn [source_text](https://docs.rs#method.source_text)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/proc_macro2/lib.rs.html#564-566)

#### pub fn [source_text](https://docs.rs#method.source_text)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>

Returns the source text behind a span. This preserves the original source code, including spaces and comments. It only returns a result if the span corresponds to real source code.

Note: The observable result of a macro should only rely on the tokens and not on this source text. The result of this function is a best effort to be used for diagnostics only.

# Delimiter in proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0.23/enum.Delimiter.html

```
pub enum Delimiter {
    Parenthesis,
    Brace,
    Bracket,
    None,
}
```
## Expand description

Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Parenthesis)

### Parenthesis

`( ... )`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Brace)

### Brace

`{ ... }`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Bracket)

### Bracket

`[ ... ]`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.None)

### None

`∅ ... ∅`

An invisible delimiter, that may, for example, appear around tokens
coming from a “macro variable” `$var`. It is important to preserve
operator priorities in cases like `$var * 3` where `$var` is `1 + 2`.
Invisible delimiters may not survive roundtrip of a token stream through
a string.

Note: rustc currently can ignore the grouping of tokens delimited by `None` in the output
of a proc_macro. Only `None`-delimited groups created by a macro_rules macro in the input
of a proc_macro macro are preserved, and only in very specific circumstances.
Any `None`-delimited groups (re)created by a proc_macro will therefore not preserve
operator priorities as indicated above. The other `Delimiter` variants should be used
instead in this context. This is a rustc bug. For details, see
[rust-lang/rust#67062](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/67062).

pub enum EscapeError {

`procmacro2_semver_exempt`## Expand description

Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.

Mostly relating to malformed escape sequences, but also a few other problems.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ZeroChars)

### ZeroChars

Expected 1 char, but 0 were found.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.MoreThanOneChar)

### MoreThanOneChar

Expected 1 char, but more than 1 were found.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LoneSlash)

Escaped ’' character without continuation.

Invalid escape character (e.g. ‘\z’).

Raw ‘\r’ encountered in raw string.

# proc-macro2-diagnostics 0.10.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/proc-macro2-diagnostics/0.10.1

Diagnostics for stable and nightly proc-macros!

## Usage

- Depend on the library in your proc-macro.

```
[]
 = "0.10"
```
- Import `SpanDiagnosticExt`and use its methods on a`proc_macro2::Span`to create`Diagnostic`s:

```
use Spanned;
use TokenStream;
use ;
```
- If there's an error, emit the diagnostic as tokens:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
```
This does the right thing on nightly *or* stable.

### Caveats

On stable, due to limitations, any top-level, non-error diagnostics are
emitted as errors. This will abort compilation. To avoid this, you may want
to `cfg`-gate emitting non-error diagnostics to nightly.

### Colors

By default, error messages are colored on stable. To disable, disable default features:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.10",  = false }
```
The compiler always colors diagnostics on nightly.

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT License ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2.0/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Abi](https://docs.rs/struct.Abi.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The binary interface of a function: `extern "C"`.
- [Angle](https://docs.rs/struct.AngleBracketedGenericArguments.html)- Bracketed - Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed arguments of a path segment: the `<K, V>`in`HashMap<K, V>`.
- [Arm](https://docs.rs/struct.Arm.html)- `full`
- One arm of a `match`expression:`0..=10 => { return true; }`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocConst.html)- Const - `derive`or- `full`
- An equality constraint on an associated constant: the `PANIC = false`in`Trait<PANIC = false>`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A binding (equality constraint) on an associated type: the `Item = u8`in`Iterator<Item = u8>`.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.Attribute.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An attribute, like `#[repr(transparent)]`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareFnArg.html)- FnArg - `derive`or- `full`
- An argument in a function type: the `usize`in`fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareVariadic.html)- Variadic - `derive`or- `full`
- The variadic argument of a function pointer like `fn(usize, ...)`.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)- `full`
- A braced block containing Rust statements.
- [Bound](https://docs.rs/struct.BoundLifetimes.html)- Lifetimes - `derive`or- `full`
- A set of bound lifetimes: `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A const generic parameter: `const LENGTH: usize`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.Constraint.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An associated type bound: `Iterator<Item: Display>`.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataEnum.html)- Enum - `derive`
- An enum input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`
- A struct input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataUnion.html)- Union - `derive`
- An untagged union input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Derive](https://docs.rs/struct.DeriveInput.html)- Input - `derive`
- Data structure sent to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error returned when a Syn parser cannot parse the input tokens.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprArray.html)- Array - `full`
- A slice literal expression: `[a, b, c, d]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAssign.html)- Assign - `full`
- An assignment expression: `a = compute()`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAsync.html)- Async - `full`
- An async block: `async { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAwait.html)- Await - `full`
- An await expression: `fut.await`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBinary.html)- Binary - `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operation: `a + b`,`a += b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBlock.html)- Block - `full`
- A blocked scope: `{ ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBreak.html)- Break - `full`
- A `break`, with an optional label to break and an optional expression.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCall.html)- Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A function call expression: `invoke(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCast.html)- Cast - `derive`or- `full`
- A cast expression: `foo as f64`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprClosure.html)- Closure - `full`
- A closure expression: `|a, b| a + b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprConst.html)- Const - `full`
- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprContinue.html)- Continue - `full`
- A `continue`, with an optional label.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprField.html)- Field - `derive`or- `full`
- Access of a named struct field (`obj.k`) or unnamed tuple struct field (`obj.0`).
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprForLoop.html)- ForLoop - `full`
- A for loop: `for pat in expr { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprGroup.html)- Group - `full`
- An expression contained within invisible delimiters.
- [ExprIf](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIf.html)- `full`
- An `if`expression with an optional`else`block:`if expr { ... } else { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIndex.html)- Index - `derive`or- `full`
- A square bracketed indexing expression: `vector[2]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprInfer.html)- Infer - `full`
- The inferred value of a const generic argument, denoted `_`.
- [ExprLet](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLet.html)- `full`
- A `let`guard:`let Some(x) = opt`.
- [ExprLit](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLit.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A literal in place of an expression: `1`,`"foo"`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLoop.html)- Loop - `full`
- Conditionless loop: `loop { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMacro.html)- Macro - `derive`or- `full`
- A macro invocation expression: `format!("{}", q)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMatch.html)- Match - `full`
- A `match`expression:`match n { Some(n) => {}, None => {} }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMethodCall.html)- Method - Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A method call expression: `x.foo::<T>(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprParen.html)- Paren - `derive`or- `full`
- A parenthesized expression: `(a + b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprPath.html)- Path - `derive`or- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRange.html)- Range - `full`
- A range expression: `1..2`,`1..`,`..2`,`1..=2`,`..=2`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRawAddr.html)- RawAddr - `full`
- Address-of operation: `&raw const place`or`&raw mut place`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprReference.html)- Reference - `derive`or- `full`
- A referencing operation: `&a`or`&mut a`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRepeat.html)- Repeat - `full`
- An array literal constructed from one repeated element: `[0u8; N]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprReturn.html)- Return - `full`
- A `return`, with an optional value to be returned.

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprTuple.html)- Tuple - `full`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attr](https://docs.rs/enum.AttrStyle.html)- Style - `derive`or- `full`
- Distinguishes between attributes that decorate an item and attributes that are contained within an item.
- [BinOp](https://docs.rs/enum.BinOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operator: `+`,`+=`,`&`.
- [Captured](https://docs.rs/enum.CapturedParam.html)- Param - `full`
- Single parameter in a precise capturing bound.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/enum.Data.html)- `derive`
- The storage of a struct, enum or union data structure.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A Rust expression.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/enum.FieldMutability.html)- Mutability - `derive`or- `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Fields](https://docs.rs/enum.Fields.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Data stored within an enum variant or struct.
- [FnArg](https://docs.rs/enum.FnArg.html)- `full`
- An argument in a function signature: the `n: usize`in`fn f(n: usize)`.
- [Foreign](https://docs.rs/enum.ForeignItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an `extern`block.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericArgument.html)- Argument - `derive`or- `full`
- An individual generic argument, like `'a`,`T`, or`Item = T`.
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/enum.GenericParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A generic type parameter, lifetime, or const generic: `T: Into<String>`,`'a: 'b`,`const LEN: usize`.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item within an impl block.
- [Impl](https://docs.rs/enum.ImplRestriction.html)- Restriction - `full`
- Unused, but reserved for RFC 3323 restrictions.
- [Item](https://docs.rs/enum.Item.html)- `full`
- Things that can appear directly inside of a module or scope.
- [Lit](https://docs.rs/enum.Lit.html)
- A Rust literal such as a string or integer or boolean.
- [Macro](https://docs.rs/enum.MacroDelimiter.html)- Delimiter - `derive`or- `full`
- A grouping token that surrounds a macro body: `m!(...)`or`m!{...}`or`m![...]`.
- [Member](https://docs.rs/enum.Member.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A struct or tuple struct field accessed in a struct literal or field expression.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/enum.Meta.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- Content of a compile-time structured attribute.
- [Pat](https://docs.rs/enum.Pat.html)- `full`
- A pattern in a local binding, function signature, match expression, or various other places.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/enum.PathArguments.html)- Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed or parenthesized arguments of a path segment.
- [Pointer](https://docs.rs/enum.PointerMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- Mutability of a raw pointer (`*const T`,`*mut T`), in which non-mutable isn’t the implicit default.
- [Range](https://docs.rs/enum.RangeLimits.html)- Limits - `full`
- Limit types of a range, inclusive or exclusive.
- [Return](https://docs.rs/enum.ReturnType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- Return type of a function signature.
- [Static](https://docs.rs/enum.StaticMutability.html)- Mutability - `full`
- The mutability of an `Item::Static`or`ForeignItem::Static`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/enum.Stmt.html)- `full`
- A statement, usually ending in a semicolon.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitBoundModifier.html)- Bound - Modifier - `derive`or- `full`
- A modifier on a trait bound, currently only used for the `?`in`?Sized`.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.TraitItem.html)- Item - `full`
- An item declaration within the definition of a trait.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.Type.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The possible types that a Rust value could have.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeParamBound.html)- Param - Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait or lifetime used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [UnOp](https://docs.rs/enum.UnOp.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A unary operator: `*`,`!`,`-`.
- [UseTree](https://docs.rs/enum.UseTree.html)- `full`
- A suffix of an import tree in a `use`item:`Type as Renamed`or`*`.
- [Visibility](https://docs.rs/enum.Visibility.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The visibility level of an item: inherited or `pub`or`pub(restricted)`.
- [Where](https://docs.rs/enum.WherePredicate.html)- Predicate - `derive`or- `full`
- A single predicate in a `where`clause:`T: Deserialize<'de>`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

# yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.0-rc/

## Expand description

A dead simple ANSI terminal color painting library.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Why *y*et another *ANSI* terminal coloring library? Here are some reasons:

- This library makes simple things *simple*:`use``Paint`
- Zero dependencies by default. It really is simple.
- Zero allocations except as needed by opt-in [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping).
- [Automatic Windows support](https://docs.rs#windows)for the vast majority (95%+) of Windows users.
- [Featureful](https://docs.rs#crate-features), no-- `no_std`- `alloc`, support with- `default-features = false`.
- `Style`constructors are- `const`
- *Any*type implementing a formatting trait can be styled, not just strings.
- Styling can be [enabled](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html)and[disabled](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)globally and[dynamically](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html), on the fly.
- A `Style`can be predicated on arbitrary[conditions](https://docs.rs#per-style).
- Formatting specifiers like `{:x}`and`{:08b}`are supported and preserved!
- [Built-in (optional) conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions)for- [TTY detection](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1)and- [common environment variables](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2).
- Arbitrary items can be *masked*
- Styling can *wrap*
- Styling can *linger*
- Experimental support for [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)is included.
- The name `yansi`is pretty cool 😎.

All that said, `yansi` borrows API ideas from older libraries as well as
implementation details from [ ansi_term](https://crates.io/crates/ansi_term).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The [ Paint](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html) trait is implemented for every type. Import it and call
chainable builder methods:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
    "Ready".bold(),
    "Set".yellow().italic(),
    "STOP".white().on_red().bright().underline().bold());
```
`>` Testing,
**Ready**,
* Set*,

__!__

**STOP**The methods return a [ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) type which consists of a

[and a reference to the receiver. Displaying a](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[(via](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``print!()`,
`format!()`, etc) results in emitting ANSI escape codes that effectuate the
style.[§](https://docs.rs#uniform-const-builders)Uniform `const` Builders

All builder methods are uniformly available for [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)

`Color`[, which means you can chain calls across library types. All methods are](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``const`, allowing creations of `const` or `static` [s. A](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style``Style` can be directly applied to values with [, from](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.paint)

`.paint()`[, available for every type:](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.paint)

`Paint::paint()````
use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*};
// `const` constructors allow static `Style`s for easy reuse
static ALERT: Style = White.bright().underline().italic().on_red();
println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
    "Ready".bold(),
    "Set".yellow().bold(),
    "STOP".paint(ALERT));
```
`>` Testing,
**Ready**,
**Set**,
__ STOP__!

[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-styling)Conditional Styling

[§](https://docs.rs#globally)Globally

Styling is enabled by default but can be enabled and disabled globally via
[ enable()](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html) and

[. When styling is disabled, no ANSI escape codes are emitted, and](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)

`disable()`[values are omitted entirely.](https://docs.rs#masking)

*masked*Global styling can also be dynamically enabled and disabled using
[ whenever()](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html) with an arbitrary

[: a function that returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html)

`Condition``true` or `false`. This condition is evaluated each time a [item is displayed. The associated styling is enabled, and mask values emitted, exactly when and only when the condition returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``true`.[§](https://docs.rs#per-style)Per-`Style`

A specific `Style` can itself be conditionally applied by using
[ .whenever()](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.whenever):

```
use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*, Condition};
static WARNING: Style = Black.bold().on_yellow().whenever(Condition::STDERR_IS_TTY);
eprintln!("{}", "Bees can sting!".paint(WARNING));
```
With the above, if `stderr` is a TTY, then:
`>` **Bees can sting!**

If it is not a TTY, styling is not emitted:
`>` Bees can sting!

See [ Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html) for a list of built-in conditions which require enabling
crate features.

[§](https://docs.rs#quirks)Quirks

As a convenience, `yansi` implements several “quirks”, applicable via
[ Quirk](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html) and the respective methods, that modify if and how styling is
presented to the terminal. These quirks do not correspond to any ANSI
styling sequences.

[§](https://docs.rs#masking)Masking

Items can be arbitrarily *masked* with the [ mask()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#tymethod.mask) builder
method. Masked values are not emitted when styling is disabled, globally or
for a given style. This allows selective output based on whether styling is
enabled.

One use for this feature is to print certain characters only when styling is enabled. For instance, you might wish to emit the 🎨 emoji when coloring is enabled but not otherwise. This can be accomplished by masking the emoji:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("I like colors!{}", " 🎨".mask());
```
When styling is enabled, this prints: `>` I like colors! 🎨

With styling disabled, this prints: `>` I like colors!

[§](https://docs.rs#wrapping)Wrapping

**Note:** *Either the  std or alloc feature is required for wrapping.
std is enabled by default. See *

[crate features](https://docs.rs#crate-features).

Styling can *wrap* via [ Quirk::Wrap](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Wrap) or the equivalent

[constructor. A wrapping style modifies any styling resets emitted by the internal value so that they correspond to the wrapping style. In other words, the “reset” style of the wrapped item is modified to be the style being](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.wrap)

`wrap()``.wrap()`d.Wrapping is useful in situations where opaque and arbitrary values must be styled consistently irrespective of any existing styling. For example, a generic logger might want to style messages based on log levels consistently, even when those messages may already include styling. Wrapping exists to enable such consistent styling:

```
use yansi::Paint;
// Imagine that `inner` is opaque and we don't know it's styling.
let inner = format!("{} and {}", "Stop".red(), "Go".green());
// We can use `wrap` to ensure anything in `inner` not styled is blue.
println!("Hey! {}", inner.blue().wrap());
```
Thanks to wrapping, this prints:
`>` Hey!
Stop and
Go

Without wrapping, the reset after `"Stop".red()` would not be overwritten:
`>` Hey! Stop and Go

Wrapping incurs a performance cost due to an extra allocation and replacement if the wrapped item has styling applied to it. Otherwise, it does not allocate nor incur a meaningful performance cost.

[§](https://docs.rs#lingering)Lingering

Styling can *linger* beyond a single value via [ Quirk::Linger](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Linger) or the
equivalent

[constructor. A lingering style does not reset itself after being applied. In other words, the style lingers on beyond the value it’s applied to, until something else resets the respective styling.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.linger)

`linger()`The complement to lingering is force resetting via [ Quirk::Resetting](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Resetting) or
the equivalent

[constructor. Force resetting, as the name implies, forces a reset suffix to be emitted after the value, irrespective of any lingering applied. It can be used as a way to finalize a lingering style.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.resetting)

`resetting()`Lingering itself is useful in situations where a given style is to be
repeated across multiple values, or when style is intended to persist even
across values that are not styled with `yansi`. It also allows avoiding
unnecessarily repeated ANSI code sequences. The examples below illustrate
some scenarios in which lingering is useful:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic().linger(),
    "you".on_yellow(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "today".blue());
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are things with you__
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "you".on_yellow().linger(),
    "today".blue()); // doesn't linger; styling is reset
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are__
things with
you
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("{} B {} {} {} F",
    "A".red().linger(),
    "C".underline().linger(),
    "D", // doesn't linger, but no styling applied, thus no reset
    "E".resetting());  // explicitly reset
```
`>`  A B __C D E__  F

[§](https://docs.rs#brightening)Brightening

Most pimrary colors are available in regular and *bright* variants, e.g.,
[ Color::Red](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.Red) and

[. The](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.BrightRed)

`Color::BrightRed`[and](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Bright)

`Quirk::Bright`[quirks, typically applied via](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.OnBright)

`Quirk::OnBright`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.bright)

`.bright()`[, provide an alternative, convenient mechanism to select the bright variant of the selected foreground or background color, respectively. The quirk provides no additional colors and is equivalent to selecting the bright variants directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.on_bright)

`.on_bright()````
use yansi::Paint;
// These are all equivalent.
print!("{}", "Regular".red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright_red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright().red());
print!("{}", "Bright".red().bright());
// The `bright` quirk lets use choose the bright variants of _any_ color,
// even when the color or style is unknown at the call site.
print!("{}", "Normal".paint(STYLE));
print!("{}", "Bright".paint(STYLE).bright());
```
`>` Regular
Bright
Bright
Bright
**Normal**
**Bright**

The `bright()` quirk can be applied before or after a color is selected
while having the same effect.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

Styling is supported and enabled automatically on Windows beginning with
the Windows 10 Anniversary Update, or about [96% of all Windows machines
worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-version-market-share/windows/desktop/worldwide),
and likely closer to 100% of developer machines (e.g., 99% of visitors to
[rocket.rs](https://rocket.rs) on Windows are on Windows 10+).

Yansi enables styling support on Windows by querying the Windows API on the first attempt to color. If support is available, it is enabled. If support is not available, styling is disabled and no styling sequences are emitted.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

| Feature | Default? | Also Enables | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std` | Y | `alloc` | Use `std`library. |
| `alloc` | Y | Use `alloc`. Enables[wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping). | |
| `detect-tty` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `detect-env` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `hyperlink` | N | `std` | Enables [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)support. |

With `default-features = false`, this crate is `#[no_std]`.

Without any features enabled, all functionality except [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping) is
available. To recover wrapping *with* `#[no_std]`, set `default-features = false` and enable the `alloc` feature, which requires `alloc` support.
